body.x: A manual monitoring system can miss the first signs of danger on an industrial site, while cloud-based video management adds bandwidth costs and exposes footage outside the site. General-purpose video platforms also ship standard algorithms, so they may not recognize the hazards particular to one site.

Braincheese Co., Ltd., an edge AI and industrial safety technology startup in Gimpo, Gyeonggi Province, says it was founded in February 2024 to deal with those weaknesses. Led by CEO Minjae Lee, a certified public accountant with a business administration degree from Seoul National University, the company is taking part in FIX 2026 and was named a winner in the FIX 2026 Innovation Awards.

According to Braincheese, its on-device AI solution is built for real-time threat detection and active machine control. The company says its proprietary edge computing and sensor fusion technology operates 100% offline and forms an all-in-one safety platform that runs from automated machine interlocks when an incident is detected to automated workflow administration for environment, health and safety (EHS). It combines computer vision with several kinds of sensor data, and it describes its work as extending safety and surveillance infrastructure for smart cities and smart schools as well as industrial sites.

The product it highlights is BRC AX-cube. Braincheese says its edge SVLM layer lets it supply algorithms built to each customer's requirements instead of standard algorithms, enforces on-site storage of original video, and runs 16 channels of analysis at once to overcome compute bottlenecks. With multi-sensor fusion, it says, the system can detect and suppress special situations other products have not been able to handle.

The company describes four operating shifts. The first is reusing 100% of existing infrastructure, which it says avoids replacing it with costly AI cameras. The second is replacing bandwidth-heavy cloud streaming with local video storage, which it says lowers the risk of privacy exposure. The third is moving from simple object detection to multidimensional threat reasoning by combining body pose dynamics, spatial rules and heterogeneous sensor data, with video joined to voice recognition, odor, temperature and flood sensors. The fourth is turning passive, context-free system logs into structured safety events. Braincheese reports that its library of specialized safety algorithms grew from 20 to 40, which it says raised baseline accuracy considerably, and says that because it develops all software and patented algorithms in-house rather than using open-source algorithms, and applies four-layer cross analysis, its false-positive rate is far lower than that of competitors.

On its record, the company says it has completed deployments of smart monitoring solutions based on on-device edge AI and multi-sensor data fusion in high-risk sectors, including defense facilities, power plants, municipal smart control centers and industrial sites. The names of its Korean clients are withheld under nondisclosure agreements. Braincheese says it plans to extend supply to affiliated system integrators and subcontracted facilities, so that hazards can be detected in real time across an entire operation in line with strict industrial safety rules such as the Serious Accidents Punishment Act. It says its Korean references support international work that includes evaluations for foreign defense procurement, deployments in hospitals and care facilities, and drone-integrated border surveillance in markets including Singapore, Saudi Arabia, North America and Europe.

Its target customers are construction sites that want to prevent accidents, smart schools aiming to prevent school violence, and local control centers. The company is expanding across B2B and B2G markets, with defense facilities, power plants, municipal smart cities and educational institutions as its high-risk, high-security targets.

Export talks are under way, but the company does not list current exports. It says it wants to start in East Asian countries, where it aims to spread Korea's high-security products against low-priced Chinese competitors with weaker security. Its stated difficulty is the certification process for security products. It says it is continuing to bring in partners and will begin delivering to overseas markets in earnest once contracts are signed.

FIX 2026 is the third edition of a future-industry exhibition that links innovative technologies in future mobility, robotics, AI and ICT, and startups. It will run from Wednesday, Oct. 21, to Saturday, Oct. 24, at EXCO in Daegu. Under the theme "AI, Beyond Tech into Reality," it offers AI-based technology exhibitions, conferences and lectures by experts from Korea and abroad, and networking programs that share industry trends and core technologies.
